concept_name: Connected Bodies — One Rope, One Tension, One Shared Acceleration
source_book: NCERT Class 11 Physics Ch.5 (Laws of Motion) — table-of-contents scope only, teaching authored from first principles. The atomic concept: an inextensible string over an ideal pulley couples two bodies so they share one |a| and one T throughout, T never equal to either weight except at a=0, solved by writing one equation per body and eliminating T. Does NOT cover drawing the FBD itself (prerequisite free_body_diagram), single-body incline dynamics (deferred to block_on_incline), or multi-pulley/massive-string systems (out of chapter scope). Built on the newtons_laws_body field_3d engine (docs/NEWTONS_LAWS_BODY_ENGINE_SPEC.md), pure configuration, zero renderer edits.

real_world_anchor.primary: An elevator car and its counterweight hang on opposite sides of a pulley at the top of the shaft — nearly equal masses, so the motor only ever supplies the small difference between them. The cable's tension is neither weight; it sits between the two, and that is exactly what a connected-bodies pair teaches.
real_world_anchor.secondary: A gym cable machine: you pull one end of a cable over a pulley and a weight stack rises at the other end. One cable, one tension throughout, and the stack accelerates only while your pull beats its own weight.
real_world_anchor.tertiary: Every exam problem with two masses joined by a string over a pulley — a block on a rough table pulling a hanging mass, a block on an incline connected to a counterweight, an Atwood pair — starts with the same two facts: the string forces one shared acceleration, and its tension is never simply equal to either hanging weight.

F.name: extra applied force on body A (sandbox only)

T.formula: string tension, N — equal magnitude on both bodies by construction

N.formula: normal reaction on the surface body only (suppressed, not zero-printed, on a hanging body)

f.formula: friction on the surface body only (suppressed, not zero-printed, on a hanging body)

F_net.formula: net force on the requested body, N

formulas.shared_constraint: |a₁| = |a₂| = a and |v₁| = |v₂| = v at every instant — the inextensible string forces one shared kinematics, opposite-signed per body through the pulley
formulas.horizontal_hanging: a = (m₂g − μₖ·m₁·g) / (m₁ + m₂); T = m₂·(g − a) — θ=0 special case of the incline formula, same code path
formulas.incline_hanging_general: a = (m₂·g − m₁·g·sinθ − μₖ·m₁·g·cosθ) / (m₁ + m₂); N = m₁·g·cosθ; T = m₂·(g − a) — θ=0 recovers the horizontal line above
formulas.atwood: a = (m₁ − m₂)·g / (m₁ + m₂); T = m₂·(g + a) = m₁·(g − a) — identically equal, both hanging, no surface

constraints: |a_A| = |a_B| = a and |v_A| = |v_B| = v at every instant — the inextensible string forces one shared kinematics
T is the SAME magnitude at both ends of the string (ideal massless string, frictionless massless pulley)
T = m2*g only in the special case a = 0 (S1/S2's earned wrong belief); whenever a != 0, T != m2*g
for incline+hanging with F=0: 0 < T < m2*g always (T -> m2*g only as a -> 0)
for Atwood: T lies strictly between m1*g and m2*g (T -> the smaller weight as masses converge)
N != 0 and f != 0 only on the non-hanging (surface) body; a hanging body always reports N=0, f=0, suppressed not zero-printed
g = 9.8 m/s^2 (engine constant); mass and weight are never the same quantity in narration
the string and pulley are ideal — massless, inextensible, frictionless at the pulley — stated honestly in narration

aha_moment.statement: T equals m₂g only when a = 0 — acceleration eats the difference.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: Releasing the frictionless rig from rest: the real block slides right past its own frozen ghost, and the tension reading (13.07 N) sits visibly below block B's weight (19.60 N) for the rest of the run.

STATE_1.title: One Rope, One Motion — Both Bodies Share One Speed

scene_composition.text:
v(A) = v(B) every instant
a = 0.00 m/s² — not free fall

one rope over the pulley
→ one shared |a|, one shared |v|

tts_sentences.text_en: A block on a table is tied by a rope over a pulley to a hanging block.
Both speed readouts match at every instant, and neither one is falling freely under gravity.
One rope makes these two bodies move as a single system, sharing one shared speed and one shared acceleration.

misconception_watch.belief: Each body has its own motion; the hanging one falls at g.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: Both v readouts stay identical the whole glide, and the a readout sits at 0.00 m/s² — far below 9.8.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: An inextensible rope makes one system — one speed, one acceleration.

STATE_2.title: Every Contact Becomes One Arrow — Same T at Both Ends

scene_composition.text:
T₁ = T₂ = T
19.60 N pulls A, 19.60 N lifts B

here — and only here —
T happens to equal m₂g

tts_sentences.text_en: Read each body's arrows one at a time: the rope pulls block A forward and lifts block B upward with the same tension T.
Here — and only here — T happens to equal block B's weight, 19.6 newtons, since nothing is accelerating yet.
One rope, one number — T is identical at both ends.

STATE_3.title: Release It — Tension Drops Below m₂g the Instant a ≠ 0

scene_composition.text:
frozen ghost = the world where
T always equalled m₂g and nothing moved

tts_sentences.text_en: Imagine tension always equalled block B's weight — then nothing would ever accelerate, and this ghost would never move.
Release the real rig frictionless and it slides right past its frozen ghost, speeding up the whole time.
Tension now reads 13.07 newtons — well below block B's own 19.6 — acceleration eats the difference.

misconception_watch.belief: The string's tension equals the hanging weight, T = m₂g.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The frozen ghost never moves while the real rig slides past it, and B's tension arrow (13.07 N) visibly falls short of its weight arrow (19.60 N).
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: T equals m₂g only when a = 0 — acceleration eats the difference.

STATE_4.title: Solve It — One Equation per Body, Eliminate T

scene_composition.text:
a = (m₂g − μₖm₁g) ∕ (m₁+m₂)
a = 0.65 m/s², T = 18.29 N

tts_sentences.text_en: Write one equation per body and eliminate tension by adding them together.
That leaves acceleration a equal to the net driving force divided by the total mass of both blocks.
Here, with friction on block A, a works out to 0.65 metres per second squared and tension settles at 18.29 newtons.

STATE_5.title: Same Rig on a Slope — the Incline Steals From the Pull

scene_composition.text:
a = (m₂g − m₁g·sinθ − f) ∕ (m₁+m₂)
a = 0.43 m/s², T = 28.11 N

same coupled glide as STATE 1
now gravity and friction fight the pull

tts_sentences.text_en: Tilt this same rig onto a thirty degree slope: now gravity pulls block A back down the incline too.
That along-slope pull and friction both fight block B's weight, so acceleration shrinks to just 0.43 metres per second squared.
Tension has to rise to 28.11 newtons to keep this slower creep going.

STATE_6.title: Atwood Pair — Only the Difference Drives

scene_composition.text:
T sits BETWEEN the two weights
19.60 N < 20.08 N < 20.58 N

tts_sentences.text_en: The table is gone now — two blocks hang on either side of one pulley.
They're almost equal — 2.1 kilograms against 2 — so they only creep, heavier side falling as the lighter one rises.
One tension, 20.08 newtons, sits between the two weights — only the mass difference drives it.

misconception_watch.belief: The heavier side plummets, and each side of the rope has its own tension.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The 2.1 vs 2.0 kg pair creeps at only 0.24 m/s², and ONE tension readout (20.08 N) sits between the two individual weights.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Only the mass DIFFERENCE drives; an ideal rope has one tension.

STATE_7.title: Explore — Every Body, Every Control, All Yours

scene_composition.text:
change both masses, the slope, the friction, even push it
watch tension and acceleration answer

tts_sentences.text_en: Everything is yours now — change both masses, the slope, the friction, even push it, and watch tension and acceleration answer together.

regeneration_variants.label: Cable Machine — Pull One End, the Stack Rises
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A gym cable machine: one end of a cable is pulled by hand over a pulley, and a weight stack rises at the other end. Same coupled string, same pulley, same shared |a| and one tension throughout.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: The cable's tension is identical at both ends and equals the stack's weight only when nothing accelerates — the instant the puller's effort exceeds that balance, the stack accelerates and T falls below the stack's own weight.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same two-body rig, same pulley geometry — only the labeled world changes from a generic block-and-hanging-mass pair to a hand-pulled cable and a rising weight stack.

regeneration_variants.label: Elevator Car and Its Counterweight
regeneration_variants.physical_world: An elevator car and a counterweight hang on opposite ends of a cable over a pulley at the top of the shaft — nearly equal masses, so the motor only supplies the small difference between them.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical to the Atwood state: only the mass difference drives the acceleration, and the one shared tension sits strictly between the two individual weights.

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered connected bodies when they can (1) state that an inextensible string over a pulley forces two connected bodies to share exactly one speed and one acceleration at every instant; (2) recognize that an ideal rope carries exactly one tension value, acting on both connected bodies; (3) prove that tension equals the hanging weight only when acceleration is zero, and that T = m₂(g−a) is strictly less than m₂g the instant the system accelerates; (4) set up one Newton's-second-law equation per body and add them to eliminate the unknown tension and solve for the shared acceleration; (5) extend the method to an incline-plus-friction variant, where the along-slope component of gravity and friction both reduce the acceleration and raise the tension; (6) extend the method to an Atwood pair (both bodies hanging), where only the mass difference drives the motion and the tension lies strictly between the two individual weights.

questions.stem: A block on a table is connected by a rope over a pulley to a hanging block. If the hanging block's speed is 0.35 m/s downward at some instant, what is the block on the table's speed at that same instant?

options.A: 0.35 m/s — the inextensible rope forces both bodies to share the same speed and same acceleration at every instant
options.B: Less than 0.35 m/s, because the rope stretches slightly as it goes around the pulley
options.C: It depends on which block is heavier — the heavier one always moves faster
options.D: The hanging block always falls at g regardless of the rope, so its speed doesn't tell us anything about the other block

distractor_misconceptions.B: assumes real stretch or slip that an ideal inextensible string never has
distractor_misconceptions.C: invents a mass-dependent speed rule that violates the shared-constraint kinematics of a single rigid string
distractor_misconceptions.D: the falls-at-g misconception this state directly confronts

questions.tested_idea: An inextensible string over a pulley forces the two connected bodies to share exactly one speed and one acceleration at every instant.
questions.parallel_form_stem: Two blocks are joined by a rope over a pulley. Explain why measuring one block's speed tells you the other block's speed too.

questions.stem: In a system of two blocks joined by an ideal rope over an ideal pulley, how many different tension values does the rope carry?

options.A: Exactly one — the same tension T acts on both bodies at both ends of the rope
options.B: Two — the tension is higher on the side of the heavier block
options.C: It varies continuously along the rope's length
options.D: Zero along the rope — it only transmits force at the pulley itself

distractor_misconceptions.B: the classic 'rope pulls harder on the heavy side' error — an ideal massless rope carries one tension regardless of what's attached
distractor_misconceptions.C: invents a position-dependent tension that only a massive, accelerating rope could ever show
distractor_misconceptions.D: misunderstands what a rope's tension even is — it is the internal pull throughout, not only at the pulley

questions.tested_idea: An ideal massless rope carries one single tension value throughout, acting equally on both connected bodies.
questions.parallel_form_stem: Explain why a single tension value applies to both ends of a rope connecting two different masses over a pulley.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block hangs from a rope over a pulley, connected to a 4 kg block on a frictionless table. The system is released from rest. Once it starts accelerating, how does the rope's tension compare to the hanging block's weight (19.6 N)?

options.A: Less than 19.6 N — tension equals m₂(g−a), and acceleration eats into the weight the instant the system starts moving
options.B: Exactly 19.6 N, because tension always equals the hanging weight regardless of motion
options.C: Greater than 19.6 N, since the rope must also pull the table block forward
options.D: Zero, because an accelerating system has no equilibrium and therefore no defined tension

distractor_misconceptions.B: the PRIMARY misconception this concept confronts — T = m₂g only when a = 0
distractor_misconceptions.C: wrongly assumes pulling the second body requires extra tension beyond the hanging weight itself
distractor_misconceptions.D: confuses acceleration with the absence of any force analysis — an accelerating system has a perfectly well-defined tension

questions.tested_idea: Tension equals the hanging weight only when acceleration is zero; the instant a system accelerates, T = m₂(g−a) is strictly less than m₂g.
questions.parallel_form_stem: A hanging block accelerates downward together with a connected block on a table. Explain why the rope's tension must be less than the hanging block's weight.

questions.stem: To find the acceleration of a two-block system connected by a rope over a pulley, what is the correct method?

options.A: Write Newton's second law separately for each body, then add the two equations so the tension terms cancel
options.B: Write one equation for the whole system directly, using only the heavier mass
options.C: Only the hanging block's equation matters since it is the one falling
options.D: Solve each body's equation independently, then average the two accelerations

distractor_misconceptions.B: ignores that the elimination method still needs BOTH masses in the combined equation
distractor_misconceptions.C: forgets the surface body also obeys F=ma and contributes its own friction and normal-force terms
distractor_misconceptions.D: invents an averaging step with no physical basis — both bodies share ONE true acceleration, not two to average

questions.tested_idea: One equation per body, added together, eliminates the unknown tension and yields the shared acceleration.
questions.parallel_form_stem: Show how adding the two per-body equations of motion for a connected system removes the tension term.

questions.stem: The same two-block rig is now tilted so the table becomes a 30° incline with friction. Compared to the flat, frictionless case, what happens to the acceleration and the tension?

options.A: Acceleration decreases and tension increases, since gravity's along-slope component and friction both now oppose the hanging block's pull
options.B: Acceleration decreases but tension also decreases, since less net force means less of everything
options.C: Acceleration increases because the incline adds extra driving force
options.D: Neither changes — incline angle only affects the normal force, not the coupled motion

distractor_misconceptions.B: wrongly assumes tension tracks acceleration in the same direction — since T = m₂(g−a), a SMALLER a means a LARGER T
distractor_misconceptions.C: invents an incline force that doesn't exist for a body sliding up-slope against the pull
distractor_misconceptions.D: denies that θ enters the coupled dynamics at all, when it changes both the driving term and the friction term

questions.tested_idea: On an incline, gravity's along-slope component and friction both subtract from the driving force, shrinking a while raising T = m₂(g−a).
questions.parallel_form_stem: Explain why tightening the incline angle on a connected-body system makes the acceleration smaller but the tension larger.

questions.stem: An Atwood machine has two nearly equal hanging masses, 2.1 kg and 2.0 kg, over a pulley. What drives the system's small acceleration, and where does the tension sit relative to the two weights?

options.A: Only the mass difference drives the acceleration, and the single tension lies strictly between the two individual weights
options.B: The heavier mass's full weight drives the system, and tension equals the heavier block's weight
options.C: Each side of the rope carries its own separate tension, matching its own block's weight
options.D: The system doesn't accelerate at all unless the mass difference exceeds some large threshold

distractor_misconceptions.B: ignores that the lighter mass's weight partly cancels the heavier one's pull
distractor_misconceptions.C: repeats the 'two tensions' misconception already confronted for the coupled string
distractor_misconceptions.D: invents a nonexistent threshold — any nonzero mass difference produces some acceleration

questions.tested_idea: In an Atwood pair, only the mass DIFFERENCE drives the acceleration, and the one shared tension lies strictly between the two individual weights.
questions.parallel_form_stem: An elevator car and its counterweight are nearly equal in mass. Explain why the motor only ever needs to supply a small force.
